title: No Room for Genocide: Italian Hospitality Against Apartheid and Israeli Crimes
author: Michael Leonardi
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/0-680x383.jpeg)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/08/07/no-
room-for-genocide-italian-hospitality-against-apartheid-and-israeli-crimes/)

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/0-680x383.jpeg)  
In the summer of 2026, a quiet act of conscience in a Naples hotel room
triggered a familiar storm. An Israeli tourist booked a stay at the Decumani
Hotel De Charme through Booking.com. She received the standard automated
confirmation email. It contained a short paragraph: the property endorsed the
“No Room for Genocide” <https://bdsmovement.net/news/no-room-for-genocide>
campaign, respected the freedom and human rights of communities suffering
racist, ethnic, and social harm, and warmly welcomed Palestinians, refugees,
and all those peacefully resisting oppression in pursuit of their
internationally recognized rights.

The tourist canceled. She told Israeli media she no longer felt safe. Within
hours the hotel was under attack. Fake bookings flooded the system. Fake
negative reviews appeared from people who had never stayed there. Attempts
were made to damage the business. The owners were forced to issue public
statements clarifying that the message went to every guest regardless of
nationality, that they had never refused an Israeli client on the basis of
passport or identity, and that they had in fact hosted Israeli guests
throughout the previous year. BDS Italia issued a solidarity statement. The
campaign of defamation continued.

This is what happens when small Italian hospitality businesses refuse
complicity.

“No Room for Genocide” was launched in July 2025 by the Palestinian BDS
National Committee (BNC), the largest coalition of Palestinian civil society
and the leadership of the global Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions movement.
It was quickly taken up with force by BDS Italia and solidarity groups
worldwide. The campaign is a direct response to the ongoing genocide in Gaza,
Israel’s entrenched system of settler-colonial apartheid, and the illegal
occupation and annexation of Palestinian land. It also responds to what the
BNC describes as the wilful negligence of third states that continue to offer
visa-free entry and safe passage to those implicated in atrocity crimes while
failing to uphold their clear obligations under international law.

International law requires states to end all forms of complicity in war
crimes, crimes against humanity (including apartheid), and genocide. That
includes the duty to deny war criminals passage or haven and, where possible,
to prosecute them. With governments largely refusing to act, the BDS movement
turned to civil society and to the hospitality sector itself. The campaign’s
organizing toolkit invites hotels, B&Bs, agriturismi, restaurants, tour
operators, and cultural spaces to take concrete steps: publicly endorse the
principle that there is no room for genocide; discourage those credibly linked
to war crimes from booking; challenge the complicity of platforms such as
Booking.com and Airbnb that list properties in illegal settlements; and demand
that states terminate visa-waiver agreements with Israel and institute
effective border screenings. Participating businesses can also join the
related “Sanctuaries of Peace” initiative, declaring their spaces places of
ethical hospitality grounded in human rights rather than neutrality in the
face of mass atrocity.

The campaign does not call for the exclusion of Jews or Israelis as such. It
targets participation in and support for a regime of systematic violence. That
distinction is repeatedly erased by those who respond with accusations of
antisemitism, the oldest and most effective weapon used to shield Israel from
accountability.

In Naples the same refusal has strong local roots. Nives Monda, owner of
Taverna a Santa Chiara and now a recognized local leader within the BDS
movement, has become a reference point for the city’s hospitality sector.
After her restaurant was targeted in a high-profile confrontation over its
public adherence to Spazi Liberi dall’Apartheid Israeliana, she continued to
organize and speak out. In a message inviting other businesses and cultural
associations to join the campaigns, she stated clearly: “It is our duty to
take a stance and do what we can to end all chains of complicity that enable
Israel’s genocide in Gaza.” That sense of duty — practical, public, and
grounded in everyday work — runs through the Italian network of spaces that
have chosen not to remain neutral.

In Tuscany the pattern repeated. In May 2026 an Israeli woman booked an
agriturismo, “Le Cantine,” in Poggibonsi. The owner, Pietro Del Zanna, wrote
to her before arrival. He stated he was not antisemitic, but he could no
longer pretend that nothing was happening in Gaza. He asked her position on
the policies of the Netanyahu government. If she disagreed with those policies
she was welcome. If she supported them, she knew his view, and he would cancel
without penalty. She canceled, publicized the exchange, and filed a complaint.
Del Zanna faced online attacks and calls to boycott his business. He also
received many messages of solidarity, including from Israelis sickened by
their government’s actions.

Nearby, in the Chianti hills, the owner of Villa Moris, a B&B, displayed a
Palestinian flag and materials linked to the related campaign of Spazi Liberi
dall’Apartheid Israeliana (SPLAI — Spaces Free from Israeli Apartheid). A
Swedish couple left a one-star review attacking her as a left-wing pro-
Palestinian activist. She replied with a powerful public rebuttal: her Jewish
grandfather had lived through the Shoah and descendents of hers had been
killed in the holocaust; the values of her household were freedom, democracy,
equality, and antifascism; she had joined SPLAI out of those same principles;
and she reserved the right to refuse potential war criminals. The review was
an attempt to punish political speech and to weaponize Jewish identity against
solidarity with Palestine. Her response refused that blackmail and reclaimed
the moral ground.

These are not isolated incidents. SPLAI — Spaces Free from Israeli Apartheid —
is the Italian expression of the international Apartheid Free Zones campaign,
itself inspired by the global movement that helped isolate South African
apartheid. Promoted by BDS Italia, it invites commercial, cultural, social,
and sporting spaces to declare themselves free of complicity with Israel’s
regime of occupation, colonization, and apartheid. Members commit not to
purchase or sell products and services of companies, Israeli or international,
implicated in violations of Palestinian rights, and not to host or participate
in cultural, academic, or sporting events financed or sponsored by Israel or
involving its official representatives. By mid-2025 the network had surpassed
five hundred adherents across Italy — bars, restaurants, bookshops, ARCI clubs
(with national ARCI endorsement), cultural centers, unions, and lodging houses
— forming a grassroots infrastructure of everyday refusal. “No Room for
Genocide” extends that principle into the intimate space of hospitality. It
asks a simple question: must a bed be offered to those who have participated
in or actively supported the destruction of Gaza and the ongoing project of
Greater Israel?

The tourism industry is not neutral. Platforms that list settlement villas and
hotels profit from the dispossession of Palestinians. Airlines and cruise
lines that bring settlers and soldiers on leave help sustain the occupation.
When Italian owners of modest hotels and farmhouses refuse that economy of
complicity, they are attacked with the full force of organized Zionist
pressure: coordinated negative reviews, false accusations of discrimination,
social-media storms, and economic sabotage. The goal is intimidation. The
method is the deliberate conflation of criticism of a state and its military
with hatred of a people.

Italy’s government under Giorgia Meloni has offered no protection. On the
contrary, it has deepened military and political ties with Israel while
criminalizing forms of solidarity at home. In that climate, the courage of
small proprietors in Naples, Tuscany, and elsewhere becomes a form of
resistance. They are not powerful. They do not control ministries or media.
They simply refuse to pretend that genocide is a private matter or that
hospitality requires moral blindness.

The broader BDS movement has always insisted that ordinary people and
institutions have both the right and the responsibility to withdraw support
from systems of oppression. “No Room for Genocide” is that principle applied
to the bedroom and the breakfast table. It is non-violent. It is precise. It
is grounded in the legal obligation of third parties not to aid or assist in
the commission of international crimes. That it provokes such fury is evidence
of its effectiveness.

The hotels, BnBs, and agriturismi that have joined are not closing their doors
to Jews or to Israelis who reject the policies of their government. They are
declaring that there is no room — in their houses, in their businesses, in
their ethics, in their understanding of human dignity — for the perpetrators
and enablers of genocide and apartheid. The campaign of harassment directed
against them is an attempt to reimpose silence and complicity. It will not
succeed for as long as people of conscience continue to answer, quietly and
firmly: not here.
